Voidspire Tactics, developed and published by Rad Codex, is a remarkable indie tactical role-playing game that embraces both complexity and creativity in equal measure. At first glance, it appears to be a retro-inspired homage to classics like Final Fantasy Tactics or Tactics Ogre, but beneath its pixelated exterior lies a deeply original system that combines turn-based strategy, open-world exploration, and puzzle-solving in a single cohesive experience. Released in 2015, it marked the beginning of Rad Codex’s reputation for intricate tactical design, later continued in successors like Alvora Tactics and Horizon’s Gate. What sets Voidspire Tactics apart from many of its contemporaries is not just its mechanics, but the sense of freedom it grants the player—every class, ability, and encounter feels designed to reward experimentation and tactical ingenuity.

The story begins in the floating world of Eral, a land of islands adrift in the void, filled with strange creatures and long-forgotten ruins. You start by creating your own party of four adventurers, selecting their race, name, and portrait, and then thrusting them into a mysterious journey revolving around the enigmatic Voidspire, a tower whose presence shapes the fate of the land. While the narrative is minimalistic, told through short dialogues and environmental clues rather than elaborate cutscenes, it succeeds in creating a world that feels cohesive and full of mystery. The setting is distinctively original—there are no typical elves, dwarves, or wizards here, but rather a variety of imaginative races like the scaled Kith, the insectoid Ardent, and the faceless, mask-wearing Elt. The sparse storytelling complements the open-ended nature of the game, allowing players to fill in the blanks through exploration and discovery.

The real heart of Voidspire Tactics lies in its combat system, which is both immediately familiar and endlessly flexible. Each battle unfolds on a grid-based map where positioning, terrain, and elemental interactions all play a critical role. The turn order is clearly displayed, allowing you to plan several moves ahead, and every ability has tactical implications beyond just dealing damage. You can knock enemies into hazards, set the ground ablaze, freeze bodies of water to create bridges, or combine elemental attacks to exploit environmental conditions. The game encourages experimentation with these interactions, creating a system that feels alive and reactive. It’s not enough to have strong characters—you must also think spatially, using the battlefield itself as a weapon. Combat is challenging but fair, with an emphasis on clever planning and adaptability rather than grinding or brute force.

One of the defining features of the game is its robust character customization. Instead of locking you into rigid classes, Voidspire Tactics allows every character to freely combine abilities from multiple job types. Over time, you can unlock up to eighteen different classes, ranging from familiar archetypes like Warrior and Wizard to inventive hybrids such as the Gadgeteer, who crafts traps and devices, or the Psion, who manipulates the minds of foes. Each class offers both active and passive abilities, and mixing them leads to endless combinations. This system invites creativity—one might build a heavily armored mage who wields fire magic while shrugging off blows, or a nimble thief who relies on elemental buffs to outmaneuver enemies. Because all skills can be learned permanently, party members evolve organically, reflecting your strategic preferences rather than predetermined roles.

Outside of battle, the game’s design expands into a semi-open world that blends exploration and tactical gameplay. You can travel across interconnected maps, each filled with hidden passages, puzzles, and secrets waiting to be uncovered. Many of your combat abilities double as tools for exploration—ice spells can freeze water to create bridges, wind can clear debris, and strength-based characters can push heavy obstacles. This seamless integration of puzzle-solving and environmental interaction gives exploration real weight and purpose, transforming what might have been a simple overworld into an extension of your tactical toolbox. The satisfaction of discovering a hidden dungeon or treasure chest through clever use of abilities feels organic and rewarding, reinforcing the sense of adventure that runs through the entire experience.

Visually, Voidspire Tactics embraces a 16-bit pixel art aesthetic that prioritizes clarity and personality over spectacle. The sprites are clean and expressive, the combat animations crisp, and the color palette varied enough to distinguish each biome and enemy type. While the graphics may appear modest at first, they fit the tone perfectly and allow the game’s mechanical depth to take center stage. The soundtrack complements this design philosophy with understated but effective compositions that balance atmosphere and rhythm, heightening tension during battle and serenity during exploration. Everything about the presentation feels deliberately crafted to evoke nostalgia without being derivative—a careful homage to the golden age of strategy RPGs rather than a mere imitation.

Where Voidspire Tactics truly excels is in how it respects the player’s intelligence. It avoids hand-holding, offering minimal tutorials and trusting you to learn through experimentation. The difficulty curve is well-balanced, steadily introducing new enemy types and mechanics without overwhelming you. While the writing is concise, it’s filled with personality, often delivered through wry humor and understated charm. The characters, though lightly sketched, develop through gameplay rather than exposition—their personalities emerge from the roles you assign them and the way you play. It’s a game that values player-driven storytelling over scripted drama, letting your strategic decisions shape the narrative.

That said, Voidspire Tactics is not without its flaws. The story, while serviceable, never reaches emotional heights; it acts more as a framework for exploration than a driving force. The interface, though functional, can feel dated at times, with menus that could use more refinement. Some players may also find the pacing slow in the early stages, especially before unlocking a wider range of abilities and classes. However, these are minor blemishes in an otherwise exceptional design. The depth of its systems, combined with its replayability and freedom, ensures that even after dozens of hours, there is always something new to try or a different strategy to perfect.

Ultimately, Voidspire Tactics stands as a masterclass in indie game design—a work that prioritizes substance over flash, creativity over convention. It is a rare example of a game that gives players complete control over how they approach both combat and exploration, rewarding experimentation and strategic thinking at every turn. Though modest in presentation, it delivers a richer, more engaging experience than many of its bigger-budget counterparts. For fans of tactical RPGs, it offers everything one could hope for: challenging battles, deep customization, a living world to explore, and the satisfaction of mastering systems that always respect your intellect. It’s a hidden gem that quietly proves how imagination and good design can outshine technical extravagance, making Voidspire Tactics one of the finest strategy titles in the modern indie landscape.

Overview:
Voidspire Tactics is a fantasy strategy game in which you control a party of 4 adventurers who get mysteriously teleported into a strange place. You have to figure out why and how you got teleported there, what's going on, and how to escape.
Mechanically, each of your characters has a main class and a secondary class. At the start of the game you have only three classes unlocked--warrior, scout, and scholar. As you gain experience in these classes you unlock new classes. Your characters can switch their main and secondary class any time they are outside of combat.
Characters can use the abilities of both their main and secondary class but only gain experience in the main class. The main class also provides certain static bonuses, such as a bonus to casting spells of certain elements or a bonus to fighting with certain weapons, a movement speed bonus, a dodge bonus, etc. Experience is used to buy new abilities in the class it is earned in. In addition to active abilities, you can also buy passive abilities, and characters can equip up to 3 passive abilities at a time from any classes where they have purchased the passive ability (even if that class is not currently a primary or secondary class for them). Finally, you earn *s, which can be used to raise the base stats of your character (skill with weapons, movement speed, skill with magic, etc), and these bonuses stick with you regardless of your class as well.
The heart of the game is fighting and exploring, though there are some light elements of puzzle solving as well.

The Good:
The central mechanics here are fun and reasonably difficult even on the normal level, with a bunch of harder difficulties available for those who like a real challenge (and some easier difficulties as well, though I don't know that this game will appeal to people who just want to play through on easy for the story). The AI is pretty good, and discovering and unlocking new classes and abilities happens at a fair rate throughout the game. Later enemies have a decent array of abilities, will use healing items, will spread out to avoid AoE, and will just generally play like pretty smart opponents, even on the normal AI level (and the AI level can also be adjusted independently from the difficulty level).
By the time you've unlocked everything, the game is nearly over and you have just enough time to pick an end game build for your party and start working on it a little before you're fighting the last boss. As a result, the game feels long enough without overstaying its welcome.
There is also a lot to discover in this game. Items can be combined with each other to create new items, the environment can be interacted with in various ways, there is a good variety of different possible class builds (though some classes seemed pretty weak to me), and there are quite a few ways to mold the terrain so you can, in some cases, avoid battle or skip over parts of the game through clever use of rope, pickaxes, and other environment traversal objects. There is also some basic crafting in the game, and a nice variety of weapons that feel meaningfully different from each other, as well as quite a few secrets for those who explore carefully.

The Bad:
The UI is pretty barren and lacks helpful elements to organize your item stash, and the graphics and sound are both very basic. There is a story, but there isn't much to it. The balance feels a little off, with some classes not being especially useful compared to others. The flip side of there being a lot to discover is that the game does not always explain its mechanics very well, which may be frustrating for some players.

The Bottom Line:
This game won't be for everyone, but if you enjoy old school pixel graphics games and are a fan of tactical combat, it's worth the time and money.

Story-wise It's linear enough to not get confused where to go, with hints available if the way forward doesn't seem possible. Though it does come down to walking in a direction from the 'hub area' and coming back with an item meant for progression, the locations you have to go are all neat enough to not feel systematic which brings me to...

Exploration-wise its fantastic, backtracking when you get your hands on ways to mine or dig, going back to that cave you couldn't reach or seeing a crack in the wall in the corner of your eye, there are also false walls that you spot since the area is suspiciously funneled towards a crevice. even looking around with the arrow keys might have you seeing something that's just off in the distance that you can maybe reach. [h1]Positive[/h1]

Packed with [b]secrets[/b], it's insane, I have never seen anything like this. For instance, you dig through a suspiciously-looking wall and discover a hidden room with some loot, but then inside that room there is another hidden passage that takes you to a whole new hidden area! The game is full of secrets.

[b]Rewards exploration[/b]: it's exciting to enter a new area, because you never know what new secrets or items you'll find, but there will be something interesting for sure.

[b]Backtracking[/b]: it's fun to go back to previously explored areas once you gain new spells, skills or items, to use them to discover more secrets.

You can [b]interact with the environment[/b] in multiple ways. For instance, you can cast the "Grow" spell in a tree stomp to make it grow into a tree, then use an axe to get wood and revert it back to a stomp. Rinse and repeat, and you can get as many wood planks as you need.

The [b]class system[/b] is great. It's similar to the job system in some Final Fantasy games. You don't level up by gaining XP. Instead, you use the XP to gain abilities and skills related to your class, and you can switch classes at any time, as well as having a secondary class, so that you can use skills that are unrelated to your main class.

[b]Non-linear[/b]: you can explore the different areas in any order you please. In fact, I discovered a secret entrance to a late-game area while I was not in the late-game yet, and I could continue exploring said area without breaking the game. Excellent.

[b]Combats are interesting[/b], and the encounters are well-designed.

You can [b]adjust the difficulty[/b] at any time.

[b]Crafting[/b] is actually engaging and fun, it rewards experimentation, you can get your materials back if you don't like the resulting weapon or armour.

Pretty much [b]bug free[/b]: the only thing I found was a very minor bug with the journal: if you add a new entry to the journal and reload the game, the notification is still there. But this can be fixed by just restarting the game. That's the only bug I found.

[b]No grinding[/b] (unless you want to): the majority of the battles are a one-time thing, you win and the enemy group disappears. Only a small number of them are repeatable.

[b]Good post-battle management[/b]: if any of your characters dies during battle, they still get full experience. Also, you gradually and automatically recover your HP and MP very quickly.

Nice [b]itemization[/b]: you progressively find better items (or crafting materials) to improve your current gear. Some of them are unique.

[b]Good music[/b]: it stayed with me, it reminded me of the music in the classic SNES RPGs.

[b]Graphics[/b]: not what you play these games for, but I liked them.

[h1]Neutral[/h1]

[b]Length[/b]: it's not super short, and even though I don't like games that are too long and overstay their welcome by adding unnecessary padding, this is not one of those games. This is one of the rare occasions where I wish the game was even longer, as I have had a lot of fun and I couldn't get enough of it.

The [b]story[/b] is not the strongest point of the game (and it doesn't need to be). This is not a negative point, the game excels in other areas, and it does not need a big story. The world-building and characters you find are interesting, but the interactions with them are minimal. I don't think this is a detriment to the game, as the dev has (correctly) chosen to focus on the strong points of the game (exploration, combat, etc.).

[h1]Negative[/h1]

Small one, but [b]I wish you could add your own custom notes[/b] to the journal or the minimap, as there are many places that you know you want to go back to. I had to take notes in my computer.

It's [b]hard to understand the effect of spending points in certain skills[/b]. What's the difference in terms of damage when you have 3 in Swords vs just 1? The game won't tell you.
Similarly, the status effects are not clear either. What does "itchy" do? What is the actual penalty for "blind"? I later discovered that in order to know this, you need to hover over the tooltip of the stat while you're afflicted, but this is not intuitive.

[b]Inventory management[/b]: no easy way to keep things organised. It becomes a chore quickly. By far the worst part of the game.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

[b]Hidden gem[/b], how is this game not getting more attention? It's the most fun I've had with a game in a very long time. The dev has, at the time of writing, released another 3 games that I can't wait to play. Get this game if you like exploration, finding secrets, experimenting, and well crafted tactical combats.

I played this game twice, once years ago, once more this year (2024) after playing Kingsvein. 
So, as the first tactical RPG of RadCodex how is this one compared to the three others? It's great!  I feel like this one had charms that the others didn't. it's the one where I can say there's ALMOST a decent plot setup.  There's mystery and the dialogue choices while usually for flavor are fun. I especially like mocking Celia for failing her ambush and fleeing. But if you play these games it's not for the plot but the gameplay. Sadly the plot is never the focus, a shame because the lore made for those games would definitely support more heavy story elements. In fact, my favorite fights are often those story driven, like that ambush I mentioned. 
Now, what about that gameplay? it's tactics grid based with timed turn orders, elemental weaknesses, status effects galore and synergistic dual class system with three passives selected from any class you levelled into. It's good stuff. Some things come and go with the entries like the size of the party being only four in this one, or the cool terrain stuff of Kingsvein being the latest innovation, but  overall this is where it all began and it's solid. Also, exploration IS rewarded in this game and all the others (though less so in alvora tactics, but that one is more experimental and the most combat focused of them all). 

Here's some exploration tips: -HUG ALL SUSPICIOUS WALLS. some are fake.  
-Break some walls and dig some ground, goodies and new areas can be found sometimes. Remember that in the mines for example, you can get ore, there's even some mythril hidden away...
-Bring pitons and ropes, essential for going down holes and cliffs. and to go up cliffs you can technically pickaxe through some of them or use lattice seeds. 
-Use wood planks to repair bridges, and rungs to repair ladders
-Use ice spells on water to make walkable ice.
-Use lightning on devices and water, you'll see why easily. 
-Growth and ruin damage have uses too. Rarely though. 
-use gate spell to move to some hard to reach place. Worth it.
-Use crafting. It's worth it.

Fighting tips:
-Read skills carefully. For example, while Spell archon is unlocked through ranged classes, most of it's skills are usable with melee weapons! you can tell because the game DOES say when you're not allowed to use ranged or melee with a skill, so just assume it works when there's nothing written.
-Triggers make a spell attack, they DO NOT count as weapons for ANY skill, but simply holding one will raise the associated element damage and well, it's similar to having a melee weapon on a mage, it's infinitely reusable if you run out of MP. 
-Mixing magic and physical damage is perfectly viable in these games. I'd say this is especially true for healers and ruin magic users (unmakers only in this entry), the former because life magic scale easily and supplement well with melee, and the latter because many of unmaker's skills are melee or close range and the class synergise poorly in this entry with the other mage classes. You don't get enough star points to laser focus only on one stat, spreading around a bit CAN be optimal because the cost to level a stat WILL increase after each purchase, the exception is health and MP who only increase in cost after many purchases.
-Please do level up health and MP. In this game, where health and mp remain rather low the entire playthrough, any hit point makes a difference. It's like how it is in paper mario: low numbers mean one point of anything matters a lot more. I know waiting for damage levels seems better, but at some point you REALLY need health to not get one shot. Some bosses do EXACTLY 30 damage in an aoe precisely to discourage you from never levelling health. If you know about the white spider boss, you know what I mean. 
-You'll likely need one character with a scholar sub class equipped and levelled at all times, both for scanning weaknesses of enemies(and adding them to the encyclopedia, only way to do so in battle) but also for restoring mp through the prayer skill. Focus energy is also a decent emergency heal, Gust is a very good aoe if you focus on it, etc. 
-A healer isn't strictly mandatory if you use items religiously, but it makes life way easier. 
-You need a gatekeeper. The gate skill is useful to reach some areas, and the class is just super strong. Gate:Flood is a very good opener. Biggest aoe in the game and makes enemies weak to ice,wind and lightning.

If nothing is catching you and you're starting to wonder whether you've grown out of video games, then please give this game a try, it might just be what you need. It's not mindbreaking or revolutinary, but it's just such a well-crafted and fun experience that you can tell was made with geniune distilled passion. I came all too late to FFT and I never played any of the retro-Final Fantasy games as a kid, but this just ticked off everything I needed in a game recently.  The combat is satisfying, the world is a blast to explore (everything feels so intuitive!) and the story - which mostly stays to the side - does enough to drive you forward. The premise is also just really unique and it feels so refreshing to not set out to save to the world or fight god. Perhaps this sounds a bit overdramatic, but this game reminded me of why I love this medium of art. What I love about indie game, and what has been lost. 

I can't praise Sean Hayden and everyone else involved enough, they really knocked it out of the park! Can't wait to play the rest of the tactics series!

This is an indie tactics game that I can best describe as a mash up of Final Fantasy Tactics Advance and Divinity Original Sin 2. It has excellent exploration (like being able to use skills outside of combat creatively!) and fun, crunchy tactical combat.

Customizing your party via its class system (which is like jobs in FFTA) is heck of a lot of fun, and creates an immensely satisfying gameplay loop.

Some of the music slaps. The worldbuilding is novel. The story is serviceable. There's a surprising amount of choice in this little indie title (aka some combat encounters are outright skippable due to choices you made, or are made more difficult). There's tons of side dungeons and puzzles.

My biggest complaints are some difficulty spikes in the early and/or late game, some of the music really does the opposite of slap, and the visual style is a litttle... bare. It also costs $20 CAD which seems really high for an indie title of this productive value. So definitely look for it on sale if that price point seems daunting (for me, it'd be well worth every penny).

Overall, it's criminal this has less than 300 reviews on Steam. This is an awesome tactical RPG gem. Just make it through the first hour - trust me, it gets heck of a lot better.

看了独立游戏蜥蜴君的视频被种了草，趁着夏促果断下手。果然一开游戏就停不下来，太上头了。找到了当初玩神界·原罪的感觉，特别是游戏中的元素连锁反应和物品合成系统。这两天就全成就了，并且下单了同一个系列的地平线之门。

虽然游戏没有中文，但是用到的英文都比较简单。游戏可以窗口模式并任意调节窗口大小，旁边开个翻译软件或网页，随时查单词非常方便，而且基本玩了几十分钟就不需要再查了。

**************************************
以下内容可能包含剧透，请谨慎阅读：
**************************************
游戏最核心的就是职业构建系统。每个角色可以同时装备两个职业，并且随时可以换。战斗中，只能使用当时装备的两个职业的主动技能。任何职业的被动技能学了就能装备，不需要装备对应的职业，但是总共只能装备三个被动技能。职业除了影响主动技能和被动技能之外，还能解锁属性的升级，包括血量、魔量、脚程、武器熟练度和元素熟练度等。

要解锁高级职业，就需要一个和多个低级职业的总经验值达到一定数值。而战斗或其他方式获取的经验只会加到主职业，所以要想解锁并使用高级职业，就必须提前规划好。

游戏难度建议就选默认的难度，有一定挑战但不太容易卡关。游戏中大部分敌人打过一次就没了，所以总的经验是有限的，新手如果职业没搭配好，又是高难度的话，可能就没法推进下去了。

游戏中的装备除了打怪掉落和捡垃圾之外， 还可以自己合成（把合成书和材料同时放到砧板上）。随着游戏推进会拿到更高级的合成材料，大概是：木头->铁->骨头->钢->水晶->秘银->独特材料。独特材料包括毒牙、激光石、电器等等。博士那里可以买一个激光石和一个高级的锤子。法师除了可以使用物理武器之外，也可以使用元素宝石作为武器，这样可以利用到元素等级的加成。弩和枪比较特殊，射完之后，需要另一个回合来装填（点一下弩，再点一下自己）。

游戏大概流程是：村庄->机器墓地->收集四个飞天石->摧毁五个炮塔->回到起点取船舵->上船（注意这里上船后就再也回不去了）->去塔尖打最终boss。

机器墓地是整个游戏的中央枢纽，见了博士之后，建议先去拿轮子把摩托车修好，方便赶路。然后建议去矿坑，拿稿和铲子。稿可以打通很多道路，铲子用来挖地。见到地上有debris一定要挖一下，能挖出很多好东西。

另外见到任何东西都可以L键查看一下加入日志，包括队友、装备、物品等等。很多时候捡到东西不知道怎么用，查看一下就有提示。而且有个成就是解锁50%的日志。

遇到一些棘手的敌人打架打不过的话，可以考虑以下建议。
1.用远程风筝打法，选射手职业，优先把远程射击和脚程升满。躲着敌人视野靠近，先射敌人一箭开战。然后边退边远程射击，很多强大、手短的敌人能轻松无伤耗死。
2.法师（特别是AOE法术）一定要关注施法延迟。施法的逻辑是，选定施法地点后，施法者是可以随意移动的，但是法术落地点是固定的，敌人可以在法术落地前离开落地点，而且AI是会躲法术的，所以不注意的话经常法术放空。
3.建议队里留个sage当奶妈，回血、上守卫法术、治疗debuff。另外scholar的回魔也很实用。
4.角色朝向决定了命中率/闪避率。正面攻击容易miss，侧面和背面攻击的命中率更高。不过这游戏貌似没有暴击机制。
5.合理利用地形。AI有时候比较蠢，直线过不来的话也不会饶，可以用路障、门、窄巷等地形轻松以弱胜强。不过这游戏没有神界·原罪的铺盖那种挡路道具，能够拿得动的道具都是可以走过去的。另外sage职业有个技能可以制造路障，也非常实用。
6.消耗类道具，比如绷带、炸弹、复活药等，多留给boss战。

VT is a party-based, turn based, game featuring a large 2-d environment to explore. It features a diverse class system allowing for extremely customizable character builds. 

Pros:
[list]
[*] Mixing and matching different classes provide many interesting options for team building.
[*] The environment is quite interactive.
[*] The game has a variety of secrets.
[/list]

Cons: 
[list]
[*] Though you may continue to gain experience as the game goes on, you may only carry the powers for two classes at a time. You will quickly realize and then max the few skills you need from these classes, somewhat stunting functional character growth.
[*] Combat is mediocre at best (even with the diversity of classes), and becomes boring well before the story ends.
[*] Inventory management is a pain. 
[*] Walking around the 2-d landscape can be a chore, especially towards the end of the game.
[/list]

Summary:

I initially found VT enthralling, with my interest primarily driven by the myriad of possibilities afforded by the class system. However, my team reached its functional experience-peak quite early on, fights started to become trivial, and the grid-based combat became a repetitive chore. I had intended to finish the game, but realized I was much farther from completion than I had hoped and quit. Walking around (and backtracking as needed) the 2-d landscape on foot was tedious and I decided that I had enough.

Despite my review, I am giving this a very, very weak recommend if you get it on sale and if you lean heavily towards these sorts of games.

Overall: 5.5/10

If you can get over the very retro graphics, this game has it all for a strategic RPG: An interesting setting, great variety and atmosphere in the various environments, a soundtrack you can groove to, good equipment variety, a good range of skills and spells, and tough but fair tactical combat against tricksy foes and scary monsters.

Several areas contain repopulating enemy groups, meaning there's no risk of being stuck just 50 experience points from that one skill or level that would help you progress; if things get too tough, you can fight enemies in these places to gather money, experience, whatever you need.

Also notably, exploration feels much more organic than you would expect from this type of game; you can deploy climbing spikes and rope to descend cliffs where you like, certain walls can be broken or rubble tunnelled through with a pickaxe, bridges can be repaired, magic can be used to influence certain objects - all kinds of neat stuff. The story is decent enough, and the journey as a whole is well worth experiencing if you're at all into these kinds of games.

The game's conceit, which works really well, is that you play as a group of explorers transported to an isolated floating landmass constructed out of lands "stolen" from a variety of different worlds. What this means in practice is that the has player a wide variety of regions to explore and a reason why they can't go any further. The world exploration is a little bit The Legend of Zelda (e.g. one-way block pushing puzzles) and a little bit Ultima 7 (e.g. you dig up spots on the map with shovels, which you store in bags nested within other bags in your inventory). The game's real story, Metroidvania-like, is how the different parts of the world map connect to each other.

The game's combat and class system will be very familiar to anyone who played Final Fantasy Tactics. Combat is grid-based, turn-based, and occurs on the level map itself. Characters can switch between classes at will, and as they gain experience they can unlock new powers for those classes. The really neat thing about the system is that a character's power is more or less conserved across classes - the flat power upgrades that characters get are on a parallel track to the classes' individual skills, and apply across the character, so when a character switches to a new class they're not completely weak. I commend the game's designer for thinking through how this should work and implementing it so well.

Stuff I didn't like: sometimes inventory management was a chore, and the game's final battle felt like a little much. I understand why the inventory system is set up the way it is: you need some conscious thought around "I am going to pick up and carry that pickaxe" so that when you actually use it an hour later you feel connection between its use and the decision to take it. That said, searching through all of my bags to try to figure out where my steel bars were could be a pain. Also the game's final boss is IMO too difficult and too different from everything that came before him given that he's at the end of a one-way on-rails sequence.

But these are pretty minor. This is a good game with good genes. I'm excited to try out Horizon's Gate someday.
